object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer entity in the system, identified by account number. Every account can have subscriptions to products.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.
Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for an account, six digits sequential, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: Every account has an account number... Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: An agreement that an account pays for a product on a billing cycle. Identified by subscription ID, prefixed with SUB.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.
Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a subscription, generated and prefixed with 'SUB'.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a subscription ID... Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product offering. The system has three products: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

source_references.excerpt: We now sell three, and an account can have a subscription to each of them at once.
Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: ProductCode
object_types.definition: The identifier for a product. Currently three values: CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: The billing artefact that specifies what a customer pays and how often. Identified by plan code (e.g., CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490). Each price plan entitles exactly one feature bundle.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.
Every price plan gives you exactly one feature bundle. CORE-MO-49 and CORE-AN-490 both give you Professional.

object_types.name: PlanCode
object_types.definition: The identifier for a price plan, describing the product, billing period, and price (e.g., CORE-MO-49).

source_references.excerpt: It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: The feature bundle or tier that a price plan entitles a customer to. Identified by bundle name. Examples: Starter, Professional, Enterprise. Specifies features like number of seats, API access, SSO.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO. It's the thing on the pricing page.
Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: BundleName
object_types.definition: The unique name identifier for a feature bundle.

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's plan, with its own identity. Records the subscription, new price plan, effective date, and requester. Created when a customer changes plans.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date... It's got a change ID. It has to, because we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates.

object_types.name: ChangeId
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a plan change record.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: StartDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a subscription becomes active.

source_references.excerpt: Subscription ID. The account. The product. The price plan. Start date. End date, sometimes. Billing period. Status.
Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a subscription ceases to be active. Optional; open-ended subscriptions have no end date.

source_references.excerpt: Start date. End date, sometimes... An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled.

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The frequency of billing for a subscription. Must be exactly one of: monthly or annual.

source_references.excerpt: Billing period -- what are the values?... Monthly or annual... Never neither. Every subscription has exactly one billing period.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: The current status of a subscription. Must be exactly one of: trialing, active, past due, cancelled.

source_references.excerpt: Status?... Trialing, active, past due, cancelled... Exactly one, yes.

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a plan change takes effect.

source_references.excerpt: we write a plan change with an effective date... and when it takes effect, and those are different dates.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: Identifier of the person or system that requested a plan change.

ambiguities.description: Term 'plan' is overloaded with three distinct meanings: (1) PricePlan - the billing artifact (e.g., CORE-MO-49) specifying price and frequency; (2) FeatureBundle - the feature tier (Starter, Professional, Enterprise) defining capabilities; (3) Sales negotiated deal plan (mentioned but out of scope). The transcript suggests these are distinct concepts but uses the term 'plan' for all three, which could cause confusion during implementation. Need to establish consistent naming across the system.

source_references.excerpt: You both used the word. Priya, what's a plan?... [Priya defines price plan]... Tom: That's not what I mean by plan at all... Tom: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets... And I mean the billing artefact... So we've got two things both called plan... and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated

ambiguities.description: The constraint on one active subscription per account per product is modeled as external_uniqueness, but the transcript also mentions the system 'blocks' duplicate subscriptions at the database level and cites the Halloway incident as motivating the constraint. Need clarification on whether this is a system enforcement rule (technical constraint) or a business rule that should be modeled separately, and whether historical (inactive) subscriptions can exist for the same account-product pair.

source_references.excerpt: one active subscription per account per product... Can they have two active subscriptions to the same product?... No. The system blocks it. That was a very expensive lesson... One active subscription per account per product, enforced at the database level.

ambiguities.description: The status 'paused' is described as existing separately from the four core statuses (trialing, active, past due, cancelled) as a boolean flag, yet it 'behaves like a status' and causes bugs by overlapping with 'active'. Need clarification on whether paused is a true status (fifth value) or a separate attribute, and how it should be modeled to prevent confusion.

source_references.excerpt: Tom: There's also paused... Paused isn't a status, it's a flag... It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs. If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too... I'm going to record the four statuses as the status, and note that paused exists separately and overlaps confusingly.

ambiguities.description: The transcript discusses cancellation behavior for annual subscriptions: when cancelled mid-term, the system sets an end date to the 'paid-through date' and access continues. However, it is unclear what the business policy should be (run to term, prorated refund, or credit), and this is explicitly parked as unresolved pending finance and legal decision. The model captures the system behavior but not the intended business rule.

source_references.excerpt: Mid-term cancellation on annual plans... What happens?... Nothing happens. They've paid for the year, they keep access until December, we don't refund... [discussion of discrepancy with sales and precedent]... the system rule is clear, and what's unclear is whether the system rule is the business rule... Then I'm parking it explicitly. What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term -- run to term, prorated refund, or credit -- is undecided.

ambiguities.description: The subscription model includes a denormalized 'current price plan' field that is maintained by the plan change process. The transcript clarifies that this field exists and is synchronized with the plan change history, but it is unclear what happens if they diverge (stated as 'the change history wins and the current plan is the bug'). Need to determine if this is a derivable field that should be computed on-read, or a stored field that requires explicit synchronization logic and monitoring.

source_references.excerpt: the subscription's plan at any moment is derived... the subscription does carry a current price plan, and the change records are the history... If those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: MRR (Monthly Recurring Revenue) is described as a derived value computed from the price plan and billing period (normalized to monthly). It appears in the reporting layer but is not stored in the source system. The model correctly treats it as derived (not modeled as an attribute), but the boundary between source system and reporting layer is not entirely clear. Need confirmation that MRR is always computed and never manually entered.

source_references.excerpt: Every subscription has an MRR... It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month... Nobody types an MRR anywhere. If they did we'd have a different set of problems... I'm not going to model it as an attribute of the subscription, then, because it isn't a fact anybody asserts

ambiguities.description: A FeatureBundle is identified by its name (Starter, Professional, Enterprise), which is described as an 'ugly' identifier because there is no code. While the transcript confirms name uniqueness, it is unclear if the name is stable (never renamed) or if a bundle could change its name and be considered the same entity. For modeling purposes, we assume the name is immutable and serves as a stable identifier.

source_references.excerpt: What's the bundle identified by?... Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me... Is the name unique?... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

ambiguities.description: The transcript mentions that products are 'fixed today' at three (CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT) with a fourth in discovery, but does not specify whether the system allows new products to be added dynamically or if the set is truly fixed. The value_constraint on ProductCode is based on current enumeration; need confirmation on whether new products can be added in the future and whether ProductCode values are assigned dynamically or predefined.

source_references.excerpt: Fixed at three?... Fixed today. There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.

ambiguities.description: The transcript states that a FeatureBundle can exist with no PricePlan pointing to it (Enterprise was built two months before being priced), but it is unclear if this is a temporary state or if bundles can be permanently orphaned. Need clarification on whether every bundle must eventually be priced, or if an unpaired bundle is a valid state.

source_references.excerpt: And can a bundle exist with no price plan pointing at it?... Yes -- we build a bundle before we price it. Enterprise existed for two months before there was anything to buy.

ambiguities.description: Email is mentioned as being on the Contact (not the Account), but Contact is not defined or modeled in this session. The relationship between Account and Contact is unclear, and it is uncertain whether Contact should be included in the ORM model or is out of scope.

source_references.excerpt: Is there anything else that identifies an account? Email, company name?... Company name absolutely not, we have four accounts called 'Acme.' Email is on the contact, not the account.
A customer -- Halloway Group -- had someone in their finance team and someone in their engineering team both sign up for the analytics product, on the same account, three weeks apart.
